title: Morning Digest, Sunday 8 November 2026
intro: The US strikes Iran again while Qatar floats a bridge deal, Stephen Miller becomes Trump's chief of staff, Eisenkot gets the first shot at forming Israel's government, Russia fires 36 ballistic missiles at Kyiv before Tuesday's talks, and OpenAI raises money below its target.

items.title: US strikes Iran again; Qatar floats a bridge deal
items.body: On Friday night US aircraft hit an air-defence site on Qeshm Island, the first strikes since the midterms; Trump called them 'minor' and said talks are making progress. Iran is studying a reported Qatari plan in which the US would lift its port blockade and free some frozen funds, Iran would admit nuclear inspectors and then reopen Hormuz; Washington has not commented. Oil fell 13 percent on the week, to about 98 dollars a barrel.

items.title: Stephen Miller replaces Susie Wiles as Trump's chief of staff
items.body: Trump moved Wiles, his longest-serving chief of staff, to his political operation and named her deputy Miller, the architect of his deportation policy, who starts on Monday. It is the first big shake-up after the midterm defeat; Democrats called Miller an extremist.

items.title: Herzog picks Eisenkot over Netanyahu
items.body: Israel's president told the former army chief on Saturday that he will get the mandate, formally handed over today, after 67 of 120 lawmakers recommended him. Eisenkot has 28 days, extendable by 14; he rules out Arab-led parties, so he needs both ultra-Orthodox parties for exactly 61 seats or must try a minority government. Netanyahu warned that such a government would 'dismantle the state from within'.

items.title: Russia fires 36 ballistic missiles at Kyiv before talks
items.body: Overnight into Saturday Russia fired 36 ballistic missiles and 172 drones, mostly at Kyiv and energy sites in 13 regions, damaging a substation that links two nuclear plants to the capital and a Dnipro bridge. Moscow is sending negotiators who stalled earlier rounds to Tuesday's US-brokered talks in Abu Dhabi, and again rejects any European role or troops in Ukraine.

items.title: Trump asks the Justice Department to investigate Democrats
items.body: He accused Democrats who threaten his officials with impeachment of 'extortion', naming Senator Elissa Slotkin and writing that they should be imprisoned. A grand jury earlier declined to indict Slotkin and others over a video on refusing illegal orders.

items.title: France's fourth protest weekend
items.body: Authorities expected up to 170,000 marchers on Saturday and deployed 70,000 security personnel, banning a Yellow Vests rally near the Élysée. Prime Minister Lecornu meets unions and employers on wages on Monday.

items.title: The left side doesn't move
items.body: After Friday's shifts by SD and the Centre Party, the Social Democrats said SD's offer changes nothing because a Kristersson government would still depend on SD, and the Left Party said it will not drop its demand for cabinet seats in return for Centre support for Andersson. That makes Andersson's answer to the Centre Party's Friday deadline harder.

items.title: Russia's 'spy house' on Lidingö is empty
items.body: The last Russian occupants have left the seven-storey building, which SVT showed was used by intelligence officers under diplomatic cover; its owner, who bought it at a forced sale in 2014 and never received rent, got inside for the first time this week. The Foreign Ministry defends having protected it under the Vienna Convention.

items.title: Funding and firms
bullets: T-Unit (Daniel Ek, Martin Lorentzon) — AI platform that pulls together information from agencies and companies to help decision-makers in crises — about 50 million euros at a valuation of about 3.5 billion kronor — Lakestar, its first outside investor, plus the founders.

Sequoia closes its London office and moves its European investing to California; of its four London partners, one moves to San Francisco, while Luciana Lixandru stays in Europe as a partner after turning down the move.
items.source: Swedish Tech News citing Di, 4 Nov; The Next Web; TechCrunch, 4-6 Nov

items.title: Scheduled
bullets: Sunday 8 November: Herzog formally hands Eisenkot the mandate.

Monday 9 November: Miller starts as chief of staff; the House returns, with Massie's Hegseth impeachment resolution due Monday or Tuesday; Lecornu meets French unions and employers; G7 foreign ministers meet in Paris (to Tuesday).
Tuesday 10 November: Israel's new Knesset is sworn in; US October inflation figures; US-Russia-Ukraine talks open in Abu Dhabi (to Wednesday); French students and teachers strike.
Thursday 12 November: the caretaker government presents its budget; Sweden's extended border checks begin; UK third-quarter GDP.

Friday 13 November: the Centre Party's deadline for M and S to present full government plans, with Kristersson reporting to the Speaker around then; JPMorgan reportedly holds an investor session for Anthropic's planned listing.
items.source: &Magazine; SVT; Daily Sabah; FT via Seeking Alpha; earlier editions

items.title: Voters punished the Iran war, and Washington is reshuffling
items.body: Democrats won both chambers on Tuesday, and Republicans blamed the war and fuel prices. Since then a Republican has moved to impeach Hegseth, Wiles has been replaced by Miller, and Trump has paused full-scale strikes while still hitting Iranian targets and talking through Qatar.

items.title: AI's money got cheaper
items.body: AI stocks had their worst day in 18 months on Thursday, partly on fears that a Democratic Congress will regulate harder, and the sell-off spread to Asia. OpenAI's latest round closed at 1.25 trillion dollars rather than the 1.4 trillion it sought, Anthropic's listing is expected below earlier hopes, and voters and protesters in the US and Europe pushed back against new data centres.

items.title: Three democracies, no government
items.body: Sweden, Israel and Belgium all spent the week without a working majority. In Sweden SD gave up its claim on cabinet seats and the Centre Party set both blocs a deadline; Israel's opposition won the first chance to govern but lacks 61 seats; Belgium's king refused De Wever's resignation and sent him back to the budget.

items.title: OpenAI raises 11 billion dollars, below its target
items.body: The first close of its new round values OpenAI at 1.25 trillion dollars before the new money, with SoftBank and Abu Dhabi's MGX taking part; it reportedly sought over 30 billion at 1.4 trillion. Anthropic is still aiming to list before US Thanksgiving, raising 80-100 billion dollars at 1.25-1.75 trillion, below what investors hoped a month ago, the FT reports.
items.source: 24/7 Wall St.; The Decoder; FT via Seeking Alpha, 6-7 Nov

items.title: Microsoft shuts its AI Frontiers research group
items.body: John Langford, a leading machine-learning theorist, announced that the roughly 50-person group behind the AutoGen agent framework is finished and that he is leaving, saying Microsoft AI's leadership favours scaling over research. The post drew one of the weekend's biggest discussions on Hacker News.

items.title: Macs quietly map users' families
items.body: A researcher's tool shows that macOS has since 2022 built an undocumented on-device knowledge graph from contacts, photos, messages and Family Sharing, with machine-learned guesses about relatives. Apple says the data stays on the device, but it sits in readable database files that any app with full disk access can open.
items.source: Eighth Rank via Hacker News; ByteIota, 7 Nov

items.title: EU says TikTok's feed breaks the Digital Services Act
items.body: In preliminary findings the Commission said the For You feed pulls users into 'rabbit holes' of harmful content and ordered changes, with fines of up to 6 percent of turnover possible; TikTok calls the findings inaccurate.

items.title: Research pulse
bullets: Scientist World (Princeton): agents automatically turned 1,000 recent ML papers into runnable research tasks scored against the reproduced human method; on a ten-task test, frontier models beat it in 84 percent of attempts when improving the method and 74 percent when starting from scratch, and an 8B model trained on the traces with GRPO matched frontier-level ideas (arXiv 2611.08478, top of alphaXiv).

Learning dynamics of on-policy distillation (Oxford, EPFL): explains why a student model trained on its own outputs with a teacher's corrections can stall or degrade, and shows that ordinary offline distillation first, even with little immediate gain, makes the later on-policy stage pay off (arXiv 2611.08016).

MAC-v2 (UC Berkeley, Sergey Levine): offline reinforcement learning from camera images that plans many steps ahead in a learned world model, made stable by predicting chunks of actions and learning features for control rather than for reconstructing pixels; it beats model-free and model-based baselines on four visual control benchmarks (arXiv 2611.07245).

must_reads.title: What Huawei's Horinger data center reveals about China's compute gap
must_reads.why: Uses satellite images of cooling equipment, substations and generators to estimate one of China's largest AI data centres: about 286 MW and roughly 81,000 H100-equivalents, about 7 percent of SpaceX's Colossus 2 in Tennessee. Explains in real numbers why abundant Chinese power does not close the gap when domestic chips deliver far less compute per watt.

must_read_backups.title: You don't need long context
must_read_backups.why: NVIDIA researchers argue that the race to million-token context windows is largely unnecessary. They first show why long context is expensive: on popular open models, generating a token at 256K context costs 3.6 to 7 times more than at 16K, a gap hidden by flat per-token retail prices. Then they show that frontier models lose little or nothing on 13 long-horizon and long-input benchmarks when an agent keeps its working context short by summarising its state often and reading files selectively, and that a coding agent still works when it compacts after every single action. They end by proposing 'semantic state space models' that carry a plain-language state between steps. Both an inference-economics lesson and a provocative architectural claim.

must_read_backups.title: AI is dramatically accelerating AI research right now
must_read_backups.why: A forecaster who has spent years modelling when AI would speed up its own development reads METR's audit of Anthropic and works through what a doubling of overall progress implies: since better algorithms need both researcher labour and compute for experiments, a 2x overall speed-up means something like a 10x boost to each researcher, close to what Anthropic staff report. She then follows the arithmetic of compounding doubling times and asks whether security, monitoring and alignment checks are ready, noting that the key evidence is redacted. The accessible, numbers-first companion to the METR report.
